Traps, release and the trapper

A trap is the machine that throws targets. Traps can be manual or automatic (the Compak® Sporting rules also name semi-automatic ones). In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ the traps of a stand are lettered from left to right, as seen from the stand: A, B, C and so on (the rulebook names A to D). In Compak® Sporting the six traps are A to F, each with a letter panel.

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

The shooter asks for the target with a call: the rules name “pull” or “ready”, though in practice the words vary. In Sporting™ the referee then gives a sound signal to the trapper, the person who releases the targets. The target must leave within three seconds of that signal.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 5 · Calling for the target and the 3-second release

Compak® Sporting

In Compak® Sporting the target can be released in three ways: by hand, by remote control or by a sonopull. A sonopull is a microphone that hears the shooter's call and releases the target by itself. With release by hand the target leaves 0 to 3 seconds after the call; a sonopull waits a fixed 0.5 seconds. At international “in line” events, where each shooter goes through stations 1 to 5 in turn, only the sonopull is used, with FITASC-approved electronic refereeing and scoring.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 2 · Releasing targets: manual, remote, sonopull

Tip: A voice release has a microphone at the station. Your own voice can trigger it. On such a stand, stay silent while the shooter is ready: whisper between targets or step back.

Trap mistakes are a No Bird in both disciplines. Examples: a target broken as it is thrown, one from the wrong trap, one thrown without a call, or one released more than three seconds late. In Sporting™ it is also a No Bird if two targets come out from the traps of the same stand when one was expected. In Compak® Sporting it is a No Bird if another machine of the same field throws a target by mistake.

Key points

  • Traps: A, B, C… on a Sporting™ stand (the rulebook names A–D), A–F on a Compak field; keep Latin letters.
  • The call (“pull”, “ready”) releases the target.
  • Sporting™: referee signals the trapper; target within 3 seconds.
  • Compak® Sporting: manual 0–3 s, remote, or sonopull with a fixed 0.5 s delay.
  • Late, wrong-trap or uncalled targets are No Birds; a microphone can hear you.
Stand Talk

  • Coach Trap B is throwing lower than in the showing — tell the referee.

    Meaning: The machine's trajectory has changed; the shooter should report it before shooting.

  • Coach It's voice release here — don't chat on the stand.

    Meaning: A microphone releases targets; talking can launch one.

  • Coach The trapper was late on that one — that's a no bird.

    Meaning: The target left more than three seconds after the call.

For the interpreter
  • Keep the Latin letters of the traps when you translate: the menu and the score sheet use them.
  • Do not translate the call itself: it is a signal for the machine, not a sentence.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. In Sporting™, how long may it take for the target to leave after the referee's signal?

    1. Up to 1 second
    2. Up to 3 seconds
    3. Up to 10 seconds
    4. Any time
    Answer

    Up to 3 seconds

    A target released later than three seconds is a No Bird.

  2. What is the fixed delay of a sonopull in Compak® Sporting?

    1. 0 seconds
    2. 3 seconds
    3. 0.5 seconds
    4. It is set by each shooter
    Answer

    0.5 seconds

    The sonopull must apply a fixed, unchangeable delay of 0.5 seconds.

  3. You are on a stand with voice release and the shooter is ready. What do you do?

    1. Give the shooter a last tip aloud
    2. Ask the trapper to wait a moment
    3. Repeat the call word for him
    4. Stay silent; whisper only between targets
    Answer

    Stay silent; whisper only between targets

    Your voice can trigger the microphone and release a target nobody called.
